en: Beware of the dog (the Pompeii doorway sign).
explain: A black-and-white mosaic in a Pompeian doorway warns visitors with these words. _cavē_ is a command to one person, and what you beware of is accusative: _canem_.
distractors: _canis_ is nominative. What you beware of is the object, accusative: _canem_.
_cavēte_ is a command to several people. The mosaic speaks to one visitor: _cavē_.
_cavet_ is “he beware(s)”. A command to one person: _cavē_.

explain: A Pompeian mosaic greets “profit” (_lucrum_) as a welcome guest. Shopkeepers hoped it would come through the door. _lucrum_ is the one being greeted, so it is in the vocative, which for _-um_ nouns looks like the nominative.
distractors: _salvēte_ is said to several people. One thing is greeted: _salvē_.
_lucrī_ is genitive (“of profit”). You greet the thing itself: _lucrum_.
_lucrō_ is dative or ablative. You greet the thing itself: _lucrum_.

explain: A house at Pompeii carried this text over its door. _hīc_ is “here”, _habitat_ is “lives”, and _fēlīcitās_ is the subject.
distractors: _habitant_ is “they live”. One subject, one verb: _habitat_.
_fēlīcitātem_ is accusative. Happiness is the one who lives here, so nominative: _fēlīcitās_.
_habitō_ is “I live”. Happiness is the subject: _habitat_.

en: Tomorrow I'll give credit, today nothing.
explain: A joke told in ancient shops and bars: _crēdō_ means “I believe” and “I lend on credit”, so the sign says “credit tomorrow, nothing today”. _crās_ is tomorrow, _hodiē_ today.
distractors: _heri_ is yesterday. The joke is about tomorrow: _crās_.

explain: A love verse scratched on walls at Pompeii. _quisquis_ (whoever) takes _amat_ (loves). _valeat_ is a wish: “let him be well, let him thrive”.
distractors: _valet_ is plain “he is well”, a statement. The graffito is a wish: _valeat_.
_valē_ is a command to the person you are talking to (“be well!”). The graffito wishes this for “whoever loves”, so the verb is _valeat_.

explain: The usual opening of a tombstone. _iacet_ is “lies” (is lying down), the 3rd person singular of _iaceō_.
distractors: _iaceō_ is “I lie”. The stone talks about someone else: _iacet_.
_iaces_ is “you lie”. The stone talks about someone else: _iacet_.

en: May the earth be light on you.
explain: A wish carved on tombstones, often shortened to S T T L. _sit_ is a wish form of _sum_ (“may it be”). The wish is that the earth will not press heavily on the dead.
distractors: _est_ is plain “is”, a statement. The wish form is _sit_.
_mihi_ is “to me”. The wish is for “you”: _tibi_.
_levem_ is accusative. It describes _terra_ after _sit_, so nominative: _levis_.

explain: The famous last line of Catullus's poem to his dead brother. _avē_ is a greeting, _valē_ a goodbye: both are said to one person.
distractors: The poem goes _avē atque valē_: hello first, then goodbye.
